source.version: Journal version of record: Journal of Innovation & Knowledge 12 (2026) 100892; received 1 July 2025, accepted 11 November 2025, available online 17 November 2025 (p. 1)
source.title_on_document: AI as a cognitive collaborator: Assimilation and accommodation in human–machine teaming for innovation

supplement.where: No online supplement is referenced. Appendix A (survey instruments) is inside this PDF (p. 10).
supplement.holds: Nothing beyond Appendix A. The paper mentions 'supplementary robustness analyses treating accommodation as a continuous variable' (p. 5, Measures) but reports no numbers from them anywhere.

paper_design_summary: 371 mid-career professionals in South Korea were assigned by stratified randomization to a 2 x 2 design: GenAI (GPT-4, with a 45-minute prompt-engineering training) versus no AI, crossed with working alone versus in dyads. All did a 90-minute open-ended innovation challenge in a controlled virtual environment. Blind expert raters scored each solution for quality, novelty, and feasibility (10-point scale) and for cross-functional integration (1-7 index).

studies.label: 2 x 2 factorial experiment (GenAI x individual/team), innovation challenge

assignment.what_was_assigned: GenAI availability (GPT-4 plus 45-minute training vs. no AI) crossed with collaboration structure (alone vs. dyad)
assignment.quote: conditions were assigned using a stratified randomization procedure accounting for prior AI exposure, job function, and digital fluency.

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper recruited 371 professionals and Table 2 cell Ns (92 + 95 + 90 + 94) sum to 371. The paper does not give a count at assignment separately from the recruited count, and the N used in the regressions (Table 3) is not printed.
participants.who: Mid-career professionals from IT, manufacturing, consumer goods, healthcare, finance, and digital services; R&D 32 percent, marketing 28 percent, planning and strategy 25 percent, other 15 percent; median 12 years of work experience
participants.quote: The study recruited 371 mid-career professionals from various industries, including information technology, manufacturing, consumer goods, healthcare, finance, and digital services.

ai_tool.how_used: Participants in the AI conditions took a 45-minute training module on prompt engineering and hands-on interaction with GPT-4, then could use it during the 90-minute problem-solving phase; prompt histories were collected (p. 5, Procedures; p. 7 examples). The non-AI arms received no corresponding training.

task.description: Complex, open-ended innovation challenge, e.g., developing a novel digital product, reimagining customer service processes, or integrating sustainability principles into an existing offering (p. 5)
task.duration: 90-minute problem-solving phase (plus 45-minute training for AI arms)

eligibility.reason: Stratified random assignment of 371 professionals to GenAI (GPT-4) vs. no AI, crossed with individual vs. dyad work (p. 5); Table 2 Ns sum to 371 people (p. 6); blind expert raters scored each solution's quality, novelty, and feasibility (p. 5). Caveats for the reviewer: the AI arms also received a 45-minute training the control arms did not; the paper calls it a field experiment but it ran in a controlled virtual environment on an assigned task (coded lab_rct); several internal inconsistencies are listed under open_questions.

one_line_finding: Professionals with GPT-4 produced solutions rated higher by blind experts than those without AI, e.g., novelty 7.1 vs 5.8 for individuals and 7.4 vs 6.1 for dyads on a 10-point scale, with GenAI β = .44 (SE .13) for novelty and .41 (SE .12) for quality (p. 6, Tables 2 and 3).
open_questions: Team arms worked 'in dyads' (p. 5), yet Table 2 gives N = 95 for Team No AI, an odd number of people, and N = 94 for Team AI. The paper does not say whether team outcomes are scored once per dyad or attributed to each member, so the unit of analysis for team arms (person vs. dyad) is unclear.

Table 3 coefficients do not match Table 2 descriptives: the raw individual AI gap in quality is 1.1 points and the dyad gap 1.0, which implies a near-zero or negative interaction, yet Table 3 reports GenAI x Team β = .58 (p < 0.001). Whether β is standardized is not stated, and the regression N is not printed.

Table 6 (p. 8) reports a team effect of β = 0.336 (p < .001) for H1-2, which differs from Table 3's Collaboration (team) β = .11 (n.s.) and GenAI x Team β = .58; the text on p. 6 says teams without GenAI did not outperform individuals.
AI arms received a 45-minute prompt-engineering training module; no-AI arms received no matched activity, so the contrast bundles training with tool access.
Inter-rater reliability ICC2 = 0.51 and the number of expert raters is not stated.

The paper describes the design as a 'field experiment' but the session ran in a 'controlled virtual environment' on an assigned challenge, not in participants' ordinary work; I coded lab_rct. A reviewer may prefer online_rct or field_rct.
notes: Outcomes listed are the four expert-rated solution outcomes in Tables 2-3. Not listed because they are self-reported: positive and negative emotion change (Table 2), assimilation/accommodation strategy (survey items, Appendix A), perceived performance. Mediation results (Table 4, p. 7: direct effect of GenAI on novelty .32, indirect via accommodation .19, 37 percent mediated, 95 percent CI [.10, 0.28]) and moderated mediation (Table 5, p. 8) are mechanism analyses, not arm contrasts. The construct for quality and feasibility is coded usefulness per the codebook (quality/feasibility of a single output); no overall creativity rating is reported. Unit coded participant because Table 2 Ns count people; see open questions on the dyad arms.
